newsitem.title: ITALY: Expert says Turin shroud older than tests say.
newsitem.headline: Expert says Turin shroud older than tests say.

text.p: The Turin shroud, one of the most mysterious of Catholic relics that was saved from a fire in April, could be much older than tests have stated, an American scientific expert said on Tuesday.

Professor Alan Adler, one of two foreign scientists attending a news conference to announce new conservation measures for the shroud, said that the enigmatic cloth was "not a painting and does not date from the 14th century".

"The marks on the shroud are of exuded blood, belonging to a man who was tortured and crucified," he added. "It cannot be from the 14th century, but is much older and far more consistent with what we know of the crucifixion of Christ."

Some Catholics believe that the shroud, which carries the blood-stained image of a crucified man, was the winding sheet that wrapped the body of Christ. Adler said it was possible the shroud dated from the 7th century.

He referred to another shroud in Oviedo, Spain which had been carbon-dated to the 7th century and bore marks "85 percent consistent" with the Turin shroud, although the bloodstains on the Spanish one were more "fluid".
Adler said it was therefore possible to surmise that the Spanish shroud could have been placed on the body first and then covered by that in Turin.
"The Oviedo shroud has been dated through carbon dating to the seventh century, therefore it is possible that the Turin shroud is of the same date," he said.

After carbon dating tests in 1988, three laboratories in England, the United States and Switzerland said it was 95 percent certain that the Turin cloth dated from between 1260 and 1390, suggesting it was a mediaeval fake.
Those results were not universally accepted by the scientific community.
Historically, the shroud can be traced no further than 1357 when crusaders were believed to have brought the 4.4 by 1.4 metre (14.5 by 4.6 foot) cloth to France from the Middle East.
Cardinal Giovanni Saldarini of Turin said in April that he would not seek new carbon-14 dating tests on the shroud before it was next put on display to the public in 1998.
Tuesday's news conference also announced new conservation measures to preserve the shroud from damage.

Austrian scientist Mechthild Flury-Lemberg said the shroud, which has been kept furled on a wooden roller in a silver case to prevent it from being damaged by sunlight or air pollution, needed to be stored in a very different way.
"The linen that was originally white is getting yellower and before long the image that is on the shroud will be no longer distinguishable from the cloth," she said.
"The rolling and unrolling is damaging, it causes wear and there is a problem of oxidisation."
Before the shroud is put on view next year, a new case of bullet-proof glass will be built and filled with inert gas. The shroud will be kept flat and fully extended.
The news conference was told that there was as yet no decision on where the shroud would be kept.
It was previously kept in a 15th-century chapel in Turin's Renaissance cathedral that was devastated by fire on April 12.
Firemen managed to save it after smashing through a bullet-proof glass screen with a sledgehammer.
Saldarini said in April that the authorities intended to display the shroud from April 18 to June 14, 1998 in the main and less damaged section of the cathedral.
The cloth has not been on display since 1978.
